opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way I tend to think about this is to start from a fairly simple framing. Right now, algorithmic progress in AI comes from some amount of research labor (human researchers at the frontier labs) combined with some amount of compute for experiments. And empirically we can try to estimate how fast algorithmic progress is going currently. Something like, effective compute from algorithms improving by maybe a few x per year, depending on how you measure it and what you count.

Then the question is: at the point where you have AIs that can fully automate AI research, what happens to the inputs? The compute for experiments doesn't change much at that moment. You have roughly the same hardware. But the labor input can change a lot. You might go from a few thousand very good human researchers to the equivalent of, say, tens or hundreds of thousands of researcher-equivalents, and those AI researchers can also run faster than humans. Maybe they work around the clock, maybe they think several times faster serially.

So the core estimation problem is something like: how does the rate of progress scale with research labor when compute is held roughly fixed? And there are a few key parameters there. One is how much parallel labor helps versus hitting diminishing returns. If you just add more and more researchers, you get a lot of duplicated effort and coordination costs, so the returns are probably sublinear. People often model it with some exponent less than one on labor. Another is how much serial speed matters, because a lot of research is bottlenecked on sequential insight, so being able to think faster is quite valuable in a way that's distinct from just having more people.

And then the big one is how bottlenecked you are by compute for experiments. If you think progress is mostly limited by running experiments, then massively increasing labor doesn't help that much. You'd get maybe a modest speedup. But I think there's a decent case that much more and better labor can substitute for compute to a meaningful degree. You can run smaller, more carefully designed experiments, you can be much more careful about what you run, you can extract more from each experiment, you can do more theoretical work, and you can optimize the code and infrastructure a lot more. So I don't think the compute bottleneck is anywhere near total.

When I put these together, my rough sense is that at the point of full automation of AI research, you'd plausibly get an initial speedup in algorithmic progress of something like, I don't know, maybe 5x to 20x or so relative to the current human-driven pace, with quite wide uncertainty. Some people would say lower, more like 2x to 3x, if they think compute bottlenecks bite hard. Some would go higher.

And the reason the initial speed matters so much is that it feeds into the question of whether you get a software-only intelligence explosion. If the AIs improve the algorithms, that makes the AIs more capable and cheaper to run, which gives you more effective researchers, which speeds things up further. Whether that feedback loop is accelerating or fizzles out depends on the returns to research. Roughly, does each doubling of effective compute from algorithms require more or less than a doubling of research effort? The initial speed tells you how quickly you're moving at the start of that, and the returns tell you whether it compounds.

So my overall view is that the initial speed is likely to be substantially faster than today. Even on fairly conservative assumptions you get something meaningful, and it's plausible that you compress what would have been several years of algorithmic progress into one year or less early on. That's a big part of why I think the period around full automation of AI R&D is really important to prepare for.

r001.rationale: The response says algorithmic progress comes from research labor combined with compute for experiments.

r002.rationale: It mentions algorithms improving effective compute by a few times per year, but does not clearly explain progress in terms of the equivalent increase in training compute.

r003.rationale: It identifies experiment compute bottlenecks as a key question, explaining that if experiments are the main limit, greatly increasing research labor yields only modest acceleration.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about this is to try to decompose it into a few different pieces, and then be pretty uncertain about each of them.

The first piece is: how much does it speed things up to have a huge number of AI researchers that are roughly as good as the best humans, but running much faster and in parallel? So the thought experiment I like is: imagine you take the current staff at one of the leading labs, and you just make them run at, say, 30x speed, and you also have maybe 10 or 100 times as many of them. How much faster does algorithmic progress go?

And the naive answer is "30 times faster," but that's clearly wrong, because you're bottlenecked on compute. A lot of what AI research is right now is running experiments, and those experiments take compute, and the compute isn't getting faster just because the researchers are. So the question becomes: how much of the progress can you squeeze out by being smarter about which experiments you run, by running them at smaller scale, by doing more careful analysis, by writing better code, by just not wasting the compute you have?

My guess is that you end up somewhere in the range of maybe 5x to 20x faster at the point where you've fully automated things, with the compute bottleneck being the main thing holding you back from the higher numbers. And I think there's a lot of uncertainty here. I could see it being 3x, I could see it being 30x or more.

The second thing I try to do is look at what's happened historically with the ratio between labor and compute. So right now, if you look at how labs have scaled up, they've added a lot more compute, and they've also added a lot more researchers, and we can try to back out something like an elasticity — how much does adding more researchers help, holding compute fixed? That's hard to estimate, but the evidence we have suggests that labor isn't totally useless at the margin, which you'd kind of expect given how much labs pay for it. Labs are paying enormous amounts for top researchers, which suggests they think the marginal researcher is worth a lot even when compute is the scarce input.

The third thing is just talking to people who actually do this work and asking them. If you ask researchers at labs, "If you had 10 copies of yourself running at 10x speed, how much faster would your research go?", you get a fairly wide range of answers, but a lot of people say things like "well, a lot of my time is spent waiting on experiments, so maybe only 2 or 3x." And then other people say "actually, I'd just run many more smaller experiments and be way more efficient, so maybe 10x." So I think the honest answer is that there's a lot of disagreement among the people best positioned to know.

Then there's a further question, which is what happens after that initial speedup. Because once you're going, say, 10x faster, the AIs themselves are getting better, and so pretty quickly you're not just talking about "AI as good as the best human researchers," you're talking about AIs that are substantially better. And that's where you get into the question of whether there's something like an intelligence explosion, where each generation makes the next generation faster. And my view is that this is plausible, but it depends a lot on how quickly the returns diminish — how much harder it gets to make progress as you make progress. And that's a parameter we have some evidence on, from looking at how much research effort has been needed for each doubling of effective compute historically, but it's also pretty uncertain.

So to put it all together: my median guess is something like, you get an initial speedup in the range of 5x to 10x once things are fully automated, and then it potentially accelerates from there over a period of a year or two, although with big uncertainty in both directions, and with compute being the thing that I'd most expect to keep it from going crazy fast.

r001.rationale: The response describes AI progress as depending on researcher labor and compute for experiments, and says compute constrains the gains from adding researchers.

r002.rationale: It estimates speedups as multiples (such as 5x–10x) but does not express algorithmic progress in equivalent training-compute units.

r003.rationale: It makes compute limits a central question when considering many faster researchers, explaining that experiments consume compute and asking how much progress can be gained within that constraint.

astra-6.text:
I think the first thing to do is distinguish the initial speedup from how quickly that speedup itself grows. You can get a substantial increase in research output from automating researchers without immediately getting a runaway feedback loop.

For the initial speedup, I’d start by asking: how many copies of the AI researcher can you run, how good are they relative to human researchers, and how much faster can they work? But you can’t just multiply those numbers together and assume that’s the increase in algorithmic progress. Research involves experiments, and those experiments take compute and time. It also involves choosing promising directions and coordinating work, so a thousand researchers working independently aren’t necessarily a thousand times as productive as one.

One way to anchor the estimate is to ask what would happen if an AI lab suddenly had a much larger research team, with the same experiment budget. How much more progress would it make? Then you can adjust for the ways automated researchers differ from humans—for example, being able to work continuously or pursue a lot of small ideas that wouldn’t otherwise be worth someone’s attention.

The key uncertainty is how much research is bottlenecked on thinking versus running experiments. If there are lots of improvements that people could find by thinking harder about existing results, automation could produce a very large initial acceleration. If progress requires a sequence of expensive training runs, making the researchers faster helps less.

So I’d want to estimate those components separately, rather than start with a particular doubling time. And then there’s a second question: how much does each algorithmic improvement increase the supply or quality of automated researchers? That’s what determines whether the initial acceleration compounds rapidly.

r001.rationale: The response says research output depends on the number and productivity of researchers, while experiments also require compute and time.

r002.rationale: It does not explain algorithmic progress in terms of the equivalent increase in training compute.

r003.rationale: It makes the balance between thinking and running experiments a key uncertainty and asks how much a larger research team would achieve with the same experiment budget.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the useful way to approach this is to ask how much you’re increasing the effective amount of research effort, and then separately ask how that translates into progress.

Suppose you have AI systems that are roughly as good as human researchers at the relevant work. You’d want to know how many copies you can run, how quickly they work, and how much of the research process they can actually do autonomously. That gives you some estimate of the increase in research labour. But a hundredfold increase in research labour doesn’t necessarily mean a hundredfold increase in algorithmic progress. You have diminishing returns, duplication of effort, and bottlenecks around running experiments.

One approach is to look at the historical relationship between research inputs and improvements in algorithms, and use that as a starting point. The difficulty is that automated researchers might have a pretty different profile from human researchers. They might be very cheap at generating and implementing ideas, while still being constrained by the compute needed to test them. Or they might be able to do useful theoretical work that avoids some of those experiments.

I’d also distinguish the initial increase in the rate of progress from what happens after feedback kicks in. Initially, you can ask what happens if you take the AI systems you’ve just built and allocate a bunch of compute to research. Then their improvements could make the researchers themselves better or cheaper, which gives you another increase in effective research effort. How quickly that compounds depends on the size of those improvements and how long the research cycle takes.

So I’d want a model with explicit assumptions about researcher capability, inference costs, experiment compute, and diminishing returns. I wouldn’t feel very confident in a single number, but I think you can make the uncertainty a lot more concrete that way.

r001.rationale: The response treats increased research labour and compute for testing experiments as distinct inputs that jointly shape algorithmic progress.

r002.rationale: It does not explain progress in terms of the equivalent increase in training compute.

r003.rationale: It identifies experiment-running bottlenecks as a key limit on the progress produced by a large increase in research labour.
